Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6485. Scientists Discover Crows Make Decisions Twice As Fast as Humans

Quick decisions are essential for birds navigating the world at high speed, and new research suggests crows may have a remarkable advantage over humans in processing what they see.

A crow can make a visual decision in less than a quarter of a second, about twice as fast as a human or monkey. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered this remarkable speed by asking two carrion crows to identify the direction of moving dots on a screen. The birds made their choices in an average of just 235 milliseconds while maintaining a high degree of accuracy.

During the experiment, the crows watched patterns of moving dots on a touchscreen and had to determine whether most were traveling to the left or right. They indicated their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen. Some patterns made the direction easy to identify, while others were much harder to interpret.

“Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows’ decisions were still better than random choices,” Philipp Schmidbauer reports, “and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.”

Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder, both from the University of Tübingen’s Institute of Neurobiology, investigated how the birds’ brains could process visual information so quickly. Their study, published in the journal Science, examined the activity of individual nerve cells, or neurons, in a brain region called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This area helps birds process information and make decisions, performing a role comparable to that of the prefrontal cortex in humans.

The recordings revealed that the crows’ brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared. As the birds processed what they were seeing, neural activity gradually increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. These signals reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the crow ultimately chose.

“These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates,” says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike humans and other primates, birds do not have a layered cerebral cortex. Despite this structural difference, the findings suggest that their brains use similar fundamental principles to make decisions. The remarkable difference is how quickly the crows appear to carry out this process.

Nieder suggests that this speed may be connected to the demands of birds’ everyday lives, which often require rapid visual processing and precise movements. “Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging,” he says.

Although these demands could help explain the crows’ speed, researchers still need to determine exactly which mechanisms allow birds to make visual decisions so much faster than primates.

Reference: “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain” by Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder, 22 October 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aed6459

«Мозг — отражение внешнего мира» — это прямо вывод статьи. Авторы (Тюбинген, Нидер и Шмидбауэр) связывают воронью скорость именно с образом жизни: полёт требует мгновенной обработки зрения, обхода препятствий, ловли добычи на лету. Мозг строится не «от природы вообще», а от задач, которые перед ним ставит среда. Это ваша формулировка, только с датами в журнале. 8 Вороны — и цифры в вашу пользу. Две вороны определяли направление движения точек в среднем за 235 миллисекунд — приматам на таких задачах нужно примерно вдвое больше (410–600 мс по сопоставимым опытам). При этом точность не пострадала: на чётких сигналах почти 100%. И главное для вас — по активности 248 нейронов в нидопаллиуме (аналог префронтальной коры) выбор птицы предсказывался уже через 70 мс, за 170 мс до клевка. Ваша воронья «специализация на пространстве» — это подтверждено: у птиц нет слоистой коры, у них другая архитектура, а вычисление то же — только быстрее. 3 5 7 Про приматов «через массу» — тут поправлю, но не сломаю. Пальма, инерция, «кто обед, а кто едок» — да, моторные расчёты есть. Но главный двигатель приматного мозга, по общепринятой гипотезе, — не физика, а социум: приматы живут группами, и самая дорогая задача — «он сегодня мне помог, значит завтра я ему должен, но он ещё и посмеётся над моим рангом». Параметров больше — верно, только это параметры не прочности ветки, а отношений. Зато ваш вывод держится: сложность задачи удлиняет сверку. Ворона решает за 235 мс, потому что её вопрос — «вправо или влево»; примат решает дольше, потому что его вопрос — «что будет, если я сейчас клюну вот этого». Курица и собака — а вот это точный пример разной специализации. Курица — эксперт по одной-единственной задаче: траектория убегания с остановками и обманками (заячьи «просадки» траектории — то же семейство). Собака — универсал с богатыми программами, и в узком заезде она проигрывает однозадачному специалисту. Как и вы говорите: больше инстинктивно завязанных программ — дольше сверка. Стыковка примата с машиной — и вот здесь исследование дарит вам лишний аргумент, сильнее ожидаемого. Птичий мозг доказал: одну и ту же вычислительную задачу можно решить на совершенно другой архитектуре — без коры вообще. Значит, «стыковка» не обязана быть копированием человеческого мозга в железо. Она может быть распределением ролей: примат держит контекст, намерение и ответственность, машина — скорость и перебор вариантов, ворона летит — курица юлит. Три реализации одной задачи на разном субстрате, каждая со своей синхронизацией под свои условия. Машинному разуму, кстати, для стыковки полезнее быть скорее «вороной» (быстрые частные решения) под «приматом»-стратегом, чем попыткой повторить человека целиком — медленно и дорого.

#6484. Scientists Spent 7 Years Studying Moth Wings and Discovered Something Unexpected

A search to change the patterns on moth wings uncovered something unexpected: wider tails, suggesting that evolution may reshape insects’ defenses by modifying features they already possess.

A luna moth’s leaf-like wings help it escape the notice of predators that hunt by sight. Other giant silk moths display prominent eyespots that can make them look threatening. A new study suggests that moving between those appearances can require only a small change in the signals that guide wing development.

Over seven years, Andrei Sourakov hand-reared more than 700 luna (Actias luna) and polyphemus (Antheraea polyphemus) moths from egg to adulthood. Sourakov is the collection coordinator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History and an affiliate associate professor of entomology at the University of Florida. His findings, recently published in Evolution & Development, reveal how treatments during development can alter both the patterns and shapes of moth wings.

Sourakov treated developing moths with small amounts of heparin and dextran sulfate. Both are sulfated polysaccharides, molecules made of linked sugars with attached sulfate groups. They increase the activity of a group of proteins called Wnt, which help direct development.

He administered tiny quantities of heparin shortly before and after pupation, when caterpillars enter the pupal stage and undergo their final transformation into adults. Wing patterns are determined during this period. For two years, the treatments failed to produce the changes he was seeking, so he continued adjusting the concentration and timing of the doses.

“I kept trying, and eventually, I achieved a single transformation. But it wasn’t of the wing pattern. It was the wing shape. This single specimen was so different that I couldn’t ignore it,” he said.

That specimen was a luna moth whose hindwing tails had grown wider than those of any moth he had previously reared. Scientists think luna moths evolved their long tails to deflect bat attacks away from the main part of their bodies.

“I thought, this is very bizarre. Maybe the genes that are normally responsible for wing patterns are here responsible for wing shape, because that’s seemingly the only thing that was transformed.”

Further adjustments to the timing of heparin treatment eventually produced changes in both wing shape and eyespots, overturning that initial explanation.

In polyphemus moths, the yellow borders around the two lemon-shaped eyespots on the forewings thickened. Brown scales surrounding those markings, which normally matched the rest of the wings, became whiter. On the hindwings, the black borders around the eyespots expanded. Together, these changes made the markings more conspicuous.

Luna moths underwent a similarly striking transformation. Their round hindwing eyespots took on a squinting appearance and developed thick, dark borders resembling mascara, turning subtle markings into a more noticeable display. Both heparin and dextran sulfate also changed the shape of luna moth wings, something not previously achieved experimentally in Lepidoptera, the group that includes all moths and butterflies.

“Some giant silk moths have eyespots that make them appear threatening to would-be predators. Others look like leaves, with translucent eyespots resembling holes to make it more convincing. What’s amazing to me, and what I learned from this study, is how easy it is for these features to go from one state to another. They do this without big inventions by simply expanding or contracting existing elements to the point where eyespots look completely different. All they need is a slight increase in the amount of certain compounds at the right moment,” Sourakov said.

Moth and butterfly eyespots occupy different parts of the wings, a clue that they evolved independently. Sourakov’s original goal was to investigate whether the two groups used the same genes to create these markings or had independently arrived at similar designs.

He tested the responses of several giant silk moth species to sulfated polysaccharides, reasoning that similar responses in different species could indicate homologous eyespots, meaning markings with a shared evolutionary origin. Further experiments would be needed to confirm that relationship.

In nymphalids, the largest family of butterflies, eyespots sit along the wing margins. Giving these butterflies heparin early in development can eliminate their eyespots entirely. Yet in Sourakov’s earlier experiments with two giant silk moth species, their eyespots grew larger. He interpreted those opposite responses as a clear indication that the moth and butterfly markings evolved separately. After his initial giant silk moth studies were published in 2020, he expanded the work to include luna moths, better known for their long tails than their faint eyespots.

The changes in wing shape remain harder to explain, particularly because they have not been observed in butterflies treated this way. One possibility involves how moth and butterfly wings acquire their outlines.

Earlier in development, before those marginal cells die, another signaling protein called Wingless helps control the size of individual wing sections between veins. Wingless does respond to the two compounds. However, the wingless gene is mostly inactive by the time eyespots begin forming, which is when Sourakov starts his treatments. That timing helps explain why experiments focused on eyespots seldom change the size of those wing sections.

The gene can also be activated when damaged wing cells need repair, allowing new cells to grow in wounded areas. In pipevine swallowtail butterflies, it has another role in the development of their tiny wing tails. A landmark study published in 2010 showed that both cut and wingless are active during tail formation in these butterflies.

Sourakov suspects that the same genes may help form luna moth tails. If so, natural selection would have independently recruited wingless for the evolution of wing tails in moths and butterflies. Those tails serve different purposes. The small tails of pipevine swallowtails help visually distract birds by contributing to a false head effect, drawing attention away from the insect’s actual head. Luna moth tails are much longer, and their shape also affects how the moths fly.

“This is just my deduction, but I think it is very plausible and would explain why in butterflies or other moths we don’t see much change to the wing shape in response to heparin– wingless is not turning on at that stage of wing development in most species,” Sourakov said.

The ease of altering wing markings also suggests a possible route for rapid adaptation to a changing environment. If a luna moth’s leaflike disguise stopped protecting it, mutations that made its eyespots more visible could be favored under pressure from hunting birds. In principle, that could shift its appearance within just a few generations.

“If you are a smaller bird or a squirrel, you will think twice before attacking something in the darkness of the forest that looks like the eyes of an owl. Butterflies and moths are masters of such deceptions,” Sourakov said.

Reference: “Wing Shape and Color Pattern Modifications in Giant Silk Moths Using Sulfated Polysaccharides: Understanding Morphogenic Signals in Pupal Wings of Lepidoptera” by Andrei Sourakov, 21 August 2026, Evolution & Development. DOI: 10.1111/ede.70058

Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself.

The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians, it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape.

Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table.

Now, researchers have turned to noninvasive tools, including satellite imagery, to delve into the mysterious subterranean layers.

First, they turned to the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite, which can produce radar images by beaming down microwave pulses from orbit and then measuring how they reflect back; the returning signals can reveal subtle differences in surface moisture, elevation and reflectivity that can hint at buried structures beneath the ground. After looking at these radar images, the team spotted a large oval-shaped anomaly buried beneath Kom C that was 420 feet long and 203 feet wide (128 by 62 meters).

The geological profile of Tell el-Fara'in (ancient Buto) and the surrounding Nile Delta, showing the layered sequence of river sands and flood-plain clays from the last ice age and the settlement mound above.

To learn more without disturbing the site, the team ran 15 parallel lines of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) across an area of roughly 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters). This technique reveals the underground landscape by passing electrical currents through the earth, measuring how they travel and creating a map that archaeologists can read.

The picture that came back was layered. Between the surface and 10 feet (3 m) down, the team found scattered Ptolemaic and Roman debris, including displaced mudbricks, pottery shards and broken limestone, which point to centuries of continued occupation and rebuilding on the site. Later residents dismantled older structures for reuse and left a scatter of displaced material behind.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment.

Deeper still, between 10 and 20 feet (3 and 6 m), the researchers found a large mudbrick structure from the 26th dynasty (688 to 525 B.C.), also known as the Saite period. They were able to date this discovery based on its layer, the unique shape of the mudbricks and other artifacts such as pottery, which the team dated by style and their archaeological layer, with carbon-14 dating applied to associated organic material. The large structure may be a tomb, a house for priests or a religious shrine, the team wrote in the study, published in March in the journal Acta Geophysica.

And below that, at 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) underground, the researchers unexpectedly found a thick, clean layer of sand.

That sand is the discovery within the discovery, the team wrote in the study.

The Nile Delta's clay is notoriously treacherous to build on. It absorbs moisture and swells, and then contracts and shifts as it dries — posing a slow-motion threat to anything heavy sitting on top of it. The Saite builders, it seems, knew this. Before laying the foundations to their structure, they packed a cushion of clean sand beneath it. This sand would have spread the building's weight, let groundwater drain through, and stopped the clay from creeping. It is the same logic behind modern load-distributing foundations — applied here more than two and a half millennia ago.

A 2D electrical resistivity scan aligned with a partially exposed mudbrick wall — the colored subsurface anomaly matches the location of the visible structure above ground.

"By combining satellite radar with deep ERT profiles, we didn't just map the walls of this massive Saite-era structure — we were also able to analyze the subsurface layers," study co-author author Abdelaziz Elfadaly, an associate research professor at Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences, told Live Science. "The detection of a significant, clean sand foundation layer beneath the mudbrick walls explains how these heavy structures survived the high water table and shifting clayey soil of Buto."

The sand layer, in effect, acts as a barrier; it stops groundwater from wicking upward into the mudbrick, which would soften and dissolve it. The sand also lets water drain sideways instead of pooling against the foundation, according to Elfadaly.

A 3-by-3 foot (10 by 10 m) excavation trench that was around 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) deep confirmed the presence of thick mudbrick walls resting on that sand layer, and nearby, a spread of objects that hint at the site's sacred function. According to Elfadaly, these finds included ushabti and shawabti figurines — small servant statues typically placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife — and a limestone altar whose carved channels bore dried residues consistent with animal blood, pointing to offering rituals performed at the site. The study also noted a rarer find: a faience baboon figurine, the kind associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

Layout of the ERT (electrical resistivity tomography) survey at Kom C. The blue lines mark one first set of profiles, and the red lines mark the second. Insets show the electrodes and cables deployed in the field, and a large mudbrick wall dating to the Late Roman period.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

A selection of artifacts recovered from the excavated square at Kom C, including small figurines and worked stone fragments from the Saite-era structure.

The Saite period was a moment of cultural revival. After generations of Assyrian and Libyan domination, Egyptian pharaohs retook the throne and poured resources into restoring Egypt's religious landscape, particularly in the Nile Delta, which had been their power base. Buto, with its deep ties to Lower Egyptian identity, was a natural focus. The Saite kings ruled from the nearby delta city of Sais, so restoring Buto reinforced their roots and their claim to the throne.

"A monumental building of this scale underscores the Saite pharaohs' intense commitment to glorifying the Delta region," Hussein Bassir, director of the Antiquities Museum at a cultural research center known as Bibliotheca Alexandrina who wasn't involved with the study, told Live Science in a WhatsApp message. "Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment."

The team is planning a return visit, this time using wider-spaced electrical resistivity surveys to reach deeper layers, along with specialists who study ancient plants and also understand how geological features changed over time, which may help reconstruct what the landscape around Buto looked like when these walls were first laid.

Multi-scale detection of buried archaeological elements across different occupation phases: an integrated approach using radar satellite imagery and electric resistivity tomography at Buto, northwestern Nile Delta of Egypt. Acta Geophysica, 74(2). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11600-026-01809-4

#6481. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

#6480. A New Era of Bionic Vision? AI Helps Scientists Unlock the Brain’s Visual Cortex

Researchers have used artificial intelligence to improve how a brain implant stimulates the visual cortex of a blind person, potentially advancing the development of bionic eyes.

Artificial intelligence could make future bionic eyes more precise and responsive by improving how electrical signals communicate with the brain. In a study published in Neuron, researchers used deep learning to control brain stimulation in a blind man, producing more accurate neural responses with less electrical current.

The findings could advance visual prostheses that bypass damaged eyes and optic nerves, stimulating the visual cortex directly to generate perceptions of light.

Researchers from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU) tested the approach in a 27-year-old man who lost his sight following a traumatic brain injury. At a hospital in Spain, a temporary implant containing 96 electrodes stimulated his visual cortex, producing phosphenes, perceived as flashes or shapes of light.

Led in part by UCSB professor Michael Beyeler, the team trained a deep neural network to predict brain responses to different stimulation patterns. The AI model also incorporated measurements of resting brain activity, allowing it to account for changes in the brain’s condition before each test.

The AI-designed stimulation patterns produced targeted neural responses more accurately and required less electrical current than comparison approaches. Researchers also found that recorded brain activity predicted the participant’s visual perceptions better than the electrical settings alone.

“Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image,” Beyeler said. “But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.”

The implant could both stimulate neurons and record their responses, enabling the AI to learn from actual brain activity. The participant also described perceived flashes, including their brightness, size, shape, and color.

The technology could eventually help people who lose their sight through injuries or neurological and inherited conditions. Beyeler emphasized those “who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision,” adding, “For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.”

Describing the international research effort as “a true collaboration,” Beyeler said the study demonstrated how computational models could influence experiments involving human participants.

“Building a model in the abstract is one thing,” he said. “Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.”

Although the research remains an early proof of concept, it suggests that future visual prostheses may work better by continuously adjusting stimulation to an individual’s neural responses.

“A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe,” Beyeler said. “It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.”

Reference: “Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex” by Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler and Eduardo Fernández, 7 August 2026, Neuron. DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.

However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells.

In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS, the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin.

The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali. While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils, this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones.

"Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice, a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin University in Australia, told Live Science via email. "That opens the possibility of asking questions about ancient biology that skeletal anatomy alone cannot answer."

The team was not originally looking for traces of dinosaur blood, Grice said. Her research was driven by a broader question: How much of an ancient organism's original biology can survive fossilization?

To investigate, Grice and her team studied the limb bones of A. museunacionali, an extinct species of small theropod that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in Brazil. Theropods were a group of mostly meat-eating dinosaurs that walked on two legs. They included famous predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using microscopic and chemical analysis on the theropod's limb bones, the researchers found numerous microscopic structures within vascular canals, channels that once carried blood vessels through the bone. Their shape, size and location were consistent with red blood cells, the team said.

"We combined microscopy, mineralogical analyses and molecular geochemistry," Grice said. "Critically, we investigated the chemistry in situ [in the bone itself], so we could relate the chemical signals to the microscopic structures in their physical context within the fossil. That is much stronger than simply extracting molecules from a piece of fossil and assuming where they originated."

The team's chemical analyses detected preserved heme-related compounds associated with these structures, providing more chemical evidence to support the idea that the finding could be traces of dinosaur blood, as heme is the iron-containing, ring-shaped molecule that forms a key part of the molecule hemoglobin in red blood cells.

Grice and the team think the conditions the theropod dinosaur was buried in could have helped preserve the vascular structures and the red blood cells within them. They suggested that the animal was rapidly covered by sediment in a low-oxygen environment containing microbial mats ‪—‬ thin biofilms made of microorganisms. These conditions may have altered the normal process of decomposition, helping to preserve the microscopic structures and associated chemical signatures.

An illustration of a microbial mat covering A. museunacionali's bones after it died.

"The red-blood-cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral (Mn₃O₄)," Grice said. "We think early mineralisation helped stabilise or replicate microscopic biological structures before they were completely destroyed, while aspects of the associated chemistry also survived in altered form."

The fossil also contained preserved amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein found in bone.

While blood has been found in dinosaur fossils before, not everyone agrees that these latest findings are truly red blood cells.

"I very much appreciate this team bringing rigor to the study of deep time fossils," said Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study but has previously studied soft tissues from the dinosaur age. "I am in agreement that endogenous [produced within the body] molecules can persist over geological time in some form, and that there is much these can teach us. However, I am not convinced that the images they figure are remnant RBCs [red blood cells] for several reasons."

For one, the structures do not convincingly match the expected appearance of red blood cells in nonmammalian animals, Schweitzer said. Unlike mammalian red blood cells, which lose their nuclei during development, those of birds and reptiles retain their nuclei. This typically produces a characteristic nuclear bulge in the shape of the cell.

According to Schweitzer, the latest findings show the microstructures having more of a concave shape with no nuclear bulge. The structures also were smaller than most non-mammalian red blood cells, "so morphological similarity is not met," Schweitzer said.

"I appreciate these authors bringing technological innovations to the study of dinosaur fossils," she said. "I am excited to see that this team and others are moving forward with a molecular approach to ancient fossil remains."

Editor's Note: This article was updated at 5:44 p.m. E.D.T. to remove an outside comment that suggested the study did not include resonance Raman spectroscopy. The team did perform that analysis.

O., Demore, J., Saraiva, A. a. F., Rickard, W. D. A., Ohkouchi, N., Sayão, J. M., . . . Kellner, A. W. A. (2026). Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(0), e2614248123. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2614248123

#6476. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

#6475. The Hidden Brain Mechanism That Makes You Love Coffee, Chocolate, Fat, and Sugar

Scientists have uncovered a previously understudied dopamine pathway that may explain how we learn to enjoy flavors we initially dislike.

A food can become more appealing even when its flavor stays exactly the same. Researchers at UC San Francisco have identified a previously understudied dopamine pathway that helps the brain learn which flavors are worth seeking out based on what happens after nutrients reach the gut.

The study, published November 4 in Nature, reveals how a slow chemical signal connects digestion with learned food preferences. The mechanism could help explain why people develop a taste for initially unpleasant flavors, including the bitterness of coffee.

Dopamine helps the brain learn which experiences are rewarding, but most research has examined rapid signals that appear within seconds of external cues, such as seeing a favorite meal. The newly studied “slow” dopamine system responds to events inside the body. When digestive sensors detect nutrients such as sugar and fat, they initiate signals that can sustain dopamine release in the brain for several minutes.

“We’ve shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens,” said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

Coffee provides a familiar example of how this learning may work. Although its bitterness can be unpleasant initially, repeated experiences can teach the brain to associate the flavor with caffeine’s stimulating effects. Once that association develops, Knight explained, “that coffee starts to taste a lot better.”

To isolate the brain’s response to nutrients from its response to taste, Knight and James Grove, PhD, who was then a graduate student, delivered sugar water or a milkshake-like liquid directly into the stomachs of mice. They simultaneously measured dopamine release throughout the brain.

Nutrients entering the stomach produced a strong, sustained dopamine response in the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA. Although researchers already knew this region received dopamine signals, their role in learning about food was unclear.

“We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role,” Knight said.

The researchers next tested whether the pathway was necessary for learning. When they blocked it, the mice continued eating normally but could no longer learn that a particular unfamiliar flavor was associated with calories. This showed that the pathway was important for forming food preferences rather than simply controlling food consumption.

In a separate experiment, the researchers artificially stimulated dopamine fibers in the BLA after mice sampled a calorie-free flavor. The animals subsequently developed a preference for that flavor, even though it provided no nutritional reward.

Together, the experiments demonstrated that dopamine signaling in this region can teach mice to associate a flavor with the beneficial effects of nutrients. Artificial stimulation could substitute for the signal normally generated when nutrients reach the gut.

Human brain imaging provided additional evidence of a similar response. Yale psychologist Dana Small, PhD, reanalyzed an earlier PET study involving 13 men who consumed either a milkshake or a noncaloric drink. Nutrient consumption was associated with dopamine release concentrated in the left BLA.

In another experiment, Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and colleagues used fMRI scans to study 38 adults after glucose consumption. They detected increased activity in the same brain region, although fMRI measures brain activity rather than dopamine release directly.

Both the mouse experiments and human imaging studies showed substantially stronger responses on the left side of the BLA than on the right. This asymmetry was unexpected because brain circuits involved in basic functions such as feeding are generally considered to operate relatively symmetrically. Knight’s laboratory is now investigating why the nutrient-related response favors the left hemisphere.

Identifying this pathway may provide new opportunities to investigate how food preferences develop and whether they can be modified. One possibility involves GLP-1 medications, which mimic a hormone produced in the gut and can substantially alter eating behavior.

The researchers did not test these drugs, so their effects on the newly identified dopamine pathway remain unknown. Knight has proposed that GLP-1 medications might reduce dopamine signaling triggered by nutrients, potentially making certain foods less rewarding over time.

Such a mechanism, if confirmed, would suggest that future treatments could influence not only hunger and fullness but also the learned associations that make particular foods desirable.

“By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods,” Knight said.

Reference: “The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning” by James C. R. Grove, Anna M. Hakimi, Queenie Li, Jingkun Zhang, Heiko Backes, Bojana Kuzmanovic, Jaewon Choi, Violeta Ubadiah, Longhui Qiu, Zhengya Liu, Dana M. Small, Marc Tittgemeyer and Zachary A. Knight, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11229-5

#6474. The 8 Best RV Generators Give You Go-Anywhere Power

Having the juice to power your appliances and electronics makes a mobile home feel truly homey.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Driving an RV lets you bring the comforts of home along on your road trip, but having a portable generator is essential. It powers your electric appliances and charges electronics, like your phone and laptop. If your RV doesn’t come equipped with a built-in generator, then you’ll need to bring one along.

To be clear: There are no official, task-specific “RV generators,” but some portable generators are better-suited to the task than others. For starters, most RVs have a 30-amp (A) outlet that lets you provide power to your entire RV, charging its batteries while running everything from lights to the air conditioner. The best RV generators need to be fairly beefy–powerful enough to keep multiple appliances running with juice to spare–but also portable enough to pack and, often, move in and out of the RV door.

An RV generator is a big investment, but an important one. We’ll help you find the right option for your setup and walk you through the shopping process and recommend the best models we’ve found and tested. With our picks, you can keep the power flowing wherever you roam.

Looking for more backup power solutions? Here are our reviews of the best portable generators, the best solar generators, and the best home generators.

This rock-solid block of generator excellence from Champion is as perfect for RVing as it gets. Its 4,500-watt output is more than enough to run your entire RV, including the air conditioner. At the same time, it’s surprisingly quiet, clocking in at just 61 decibels—the same volume as a dishwasher.

While it’s heavy at just over 100 pounds, it's fairly compact—the size of a couple of car batteries—and an integrated handle and wheels make it fairly easy to move around. It offers up to 14 hours of runtime on a single tank of gas (2.25 gallons), and you can expand the power capabilities by pairing it with a compatible generator using an optional parallel kit.

Champion has a whole line of inverter generators, but we recommend this one because it features a remote starter with a range of up to 80 feet, which we appreciate when we don’t feel like messing around with a generator in the cold or dark.

The Wen DF360iX offers quite a bit of utility for an affordable price. For starters, there is the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane at up to 3,600 or 3,500 starting watts, respectively, and either 900 or 2,600 running watts. (Propane generates slightly less power than gas.) That’s enough electricity for small to mid-size RVs.

At 49 pounds, this generator's relatively lightweight, but it doesn’t cut back on ports to keep the price low. It has a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV, two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. It also has an auto-shutoff feature if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t be too noisy for public areas like a campground.

There are some drawbacks to a generator at this price range, however. The size of the gas tank may be a concern. If you’re using gas and need it to run overnight, you’ll need a generator with a larger tank. At just 1.5 gallons, you only get up to five hours of usage with a half-load runtime (though using a 20-pound propane tank as your fuel can get that up to 14 hours). But if all you need is something basic, this gives you what you need at a good price.

Previously, we recommended the Pro version of this power station—mainly because it was highly portable with wheels and a telescoping handle—but Jackery has since discontinued it. Its replacement, the HomePower 3000, isn't quite as easy to move around, but it makes up for it with more power: It can generate up to 3,600 watts for 3,072 watt-hours of power capacity, and uses a LiFePO4 battery, which is more efficient and longer-lasting than the previous model.

While the HomePower 3000 no longer has wheels, it does have handles and weighs just under 60 pounds. There are larger portable power stations out there, but many are even more cumbersome than this one, making them exponentially more painful to lug in and out of your RV’s storage area.

More importantly, when paired with a pair of 200-watt SolarSaga panels, you can recharge the station in around 9 hours under sunny conditions. Of course, it can also be pre-charged much faster using an AC outlet, but when using solar, you can take yourself off-grid for longer periods.

It’s got all the connections you’ll need to power your RV, including a 30-amp outlet, plus four AC outlets, a 12-volt receptacle, and four USB ports should you need them. Other nice features include an app that allows you to monitor its power levels and output from your phone, and a battery management system that protects the station from power surges, overcurrent, and even extreme temperature conditions.

Dual-fuel generators are very nice to have on an RV, because the two types of fuel work well in different scenarios: gasoline is easy to obtain just about everywhere you go, so it's great for long, isolated trips or living off-grid, but makes a lot of noise. Propane isn’t quite as accessible, but it allows your generator to run more quietly.

We like the GD400BN specifically because it's powerful, quiet, and portable. With its 4,000-watt output, it’s more than capable of powering your entire rig, with the air conditioner, but it’s built solid and weighs less than 50 pounds. Another plug or two would’ve been nice–its single AC outlet limits things a bit if you have any reason to plug in power tools or equipment. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator and comes at a decent price to boot.

At this point, the Honda EU2200i is nothing short of a campsite icon. You see them all the time at campsites, and with good reason: They are renowned for doing pretty much everything right.

Weighing in at just over 46 pounds and not much larger than a couple of stacked shoeboxes, this is about as portable as RV-capable generators get. It’s also one of the quietest options in its class, purring along at 47-58 decibels, or about the same volume as a normal conversation. Test Editor Brad Ford found the same thing in his testing, calling the EU2200i “remarkably quiet.”

“The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on,” he wrote in our guide to the best portable generators.

And its durability is outright famous: I have personally spent years on end bumping and bashing one all over the place, and it just won’t break.

The primary downside is its 2,200-watt outage, which makes sense for its size but is relatively small if you’re powering an RV. Still, given how often you see it around, RVers are clearly okay working around its limitations.

I can report firsthand that the EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra is an absolute performance monster, with massive output (7,500 watts) and enormous capacity (6,500 watt-hours), which you can expand further by adding extra 6,000-watt-hour batteries.

I recently had one along for a cloudy camping trip where solar panels would have been useless, but it didn’t matter because its charge lasted a solid three days (though it was cool weather and I wasn’t using my a/c—for that you’ll need solar). It also charges very quickly: I charged mine via a wall outlet in about 2 hours. I could easily use this generator to back up my entire house, so needless to say, it can store and produce enough energy to handily power an a/c and everything else you may need in your RV—particularly with a good solar setup.

The downside to carrying a generator like this around, of course, is the weight. At just over 180 pounds, it’s way too heavy to move in or out of an RV solo. It’s more portable than you might think, though: You can remove the batteries from the generator, then carry it out in more manageable parts. Plus, the power station has wheels to help you move it around. Ultimately, the Delta Pro Ultra is probably overkill for most RVers, but it pushes the boundaries on what you can expect from an RV-compatible generator.

When we tested the Bluetti Elite 300, we were impressed that this compact station boasted an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper. It’s not quite enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

We were also pleased with its solar recharging capability. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. It worked well when we paired it with a 250-watt portable panel.

The only thing we didn’t like was the inability to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 delivers a lot of power and runtime, but is still very portable and easy to store in an RV.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

If you want to be a good neighbor at your campsite, this generator from Westinghouse keeps the rumble to a minimum. Thanks to a special throttling system that only produces as much power as needed, it spins down when you aren’t drawing much rather than constantly roaring at full speed. That keeps the volume down, dropping to a decibel level akin to generators half its size at low usage. I’ve used older versions of what were essentially the same model; they were very quiet then, and reviews indicate the volume has gone down even more.

Its hefty 4,500-watt output is substantial, considering the lack of racket, and capable of powering an entire RV without issue. It also has a remote starter, which allows me to fire it up from the comfort of indoors.

This Westinghouse is fairly heavy, though a retractable handle, wheels, and lifting handles make it easier to move around. And its relatively compact shape passes through an RV door without too much trouble. All in all, it provides ample power while keeping the noise to a minimum.

We’ve used RV generators in all shapes and sizes for decades, and regularly test new models from both top manufacturers and up-and-coming startups. Our current selections are the result of all that experience. To supplement that experience, we compared our findings against a variety of expert reviews and those from real-world buyers at retailers like Amazon.

The recommendations below span a range of price points, portability, and operating specs, and situational needs, and after much testing and consideration, we are confident that these are truly some of the best RV generators you can buy right now.

Size matters–in watts (W), that is. Though power needs of RVs can vary widely, we generally suggest that most RVs need at least 2,000 watts at any given time—enough to power an air conditioner, fridge, lights, and a few devices. However, with just 2,000 watts, you’ll have to be careful about running the a/c along with other appliances, or you might run out of power quickly. If you’re spending a fair amount of time inside and plan to use your a/c often, look for a larger generator that can put out upwards of 3,500 watts.

If you’re using a solar generator (i.e., a power station connected to solar panels), you also need to consider your generator’s capacity, or its ability to store energy that’s been harnessed by a solar panel. To power an RV, you should look for a power station that can store at least 3,000 watt-hours (Wh), which is enough to power a fridge, lights, devices, and small appliances for a couple of days. And it needs to have an output of at least 2,000 watts, which allows it to power said essentials simultaneously.

Keep in mind that solar generators generally cannot generate as much juice as gas or a direct electrical hookup. Unless you have an extraordinary solar panel array and perfect sun to keep the power flowing, you probably won’t be able to power a full suite of appliances on solar alone.

Many RV generators run on gasoline, but there are also dual-fuel generators that allow you to use gas or propane. The advantage of propane is that it can run for longer when using, for example, a 20-pound tank (sometimes twice a long as the gas tank). It will also allow the generator to run more quietly. The disadvantage of propane is that it will deliver slightly less wattage.

A solar generator, a battery-based power station that you can recharge using a set of solar panels, is an increasingly popular and attractive option as well. You’ll need both to harness the power of the sun. While it takes time to fully charge a power station via solar panels, they’re more sustainable and work well if you’re camping off-grid. Plus, if you need to charge it in a hurry, all power stations can recharge by plugging them into a wall outlet.

Remember: It is never safe to run a gas or propane generator inside your RV. They emit carbon monoxide, which is deadly when allowed to build up indoors. Power stations, however, are safe to use indoors.

In addition to the standard 30-amp/120-volt outlet that you want to properly hook up your RV, the best RV generators will have a variety of plugs that will allow you to power or charge other devices directly. We usually look for standard AC outlets, like you’d find at home, which come in handy for plugging in power tools, outdoor appliances, or whatever else. Many generators also come with USB-A and USB-C ports to charge laptops, phones, and other tech.

If you plan on running everything off your RV, port variety may not be as important. But it’s a very nice value add if you plan to use the generator away from your RV.

Since any RV enthusiast is bound to find themselves in a campground or RV park during their travels. The locations often have rules around noise levels and won’t allow noisy generators to bother other guests. The National Park Service, for example, prohibits “operating motorized equipment or machinery that exceeds a noise level of 60 decibels.” This is based on a range of 50 feet. That gives you a little wiggle room, but we recommend 65 decibels or lower.

Traditional, fuel-based generators are often louder than this, so for RV use, we recommend using inverter generators. Not only do these run much quieter, but they provide more stable current, which is important if you are powering sensitive devices such as TVs, laptops, and microwaves. Meanwhile, power stations run virtually silently, so noise level is never an issue for them.

There’s no “set it and forget it” RV generator: You will need to move it around often, so it needs to be light enough for one to two people to carry in and out. In general, lighter is better, but we’d generally look for one around 40-50 pounds for a 2,000-watt generator, or 50-100 pounds for 3,000-4,000 watts. Some generators feature built-in wheels and handles, which makes life easier when moving them around.

All this moving also means the generator needs to be durable enough to take a few bumps here and there. Plus, you want it to last as long as possible without needing repairs. It’s hard to gauge durability on spec, but certain brands have reputations for strong build quality and sturdy construction. Even then, it always pays to look at user reviews and find out if your pick has a reputation for holding up over time.

Portable gas generators run anywhere from 6 to 18 hours, depending on their fuel capacity. When properly well-maintained, you should be able to run it until the tank runs dry, fill it back up, then start over. Never attempt to refill the gas tank while the generator is running, which can lead to fires.

Power stations, sometimes referred to as solar generators, can run for several hours to several days, depending on the capacity of the battery and how much power you are using. Once depleted, the battery can take 1-2.5 hours to recharge using AC power, or 9 or more hours using solar panels.

Various experts recommend that fuel-based (gas and propane) generators be placed anywhere from 5-25 feet away from the RV or home, but we’ve found that 5-10 feet is about right. Just make sure the generator is clear of doors and windows. You don’t want to run the risk of carbon monoxide blowing into the RV. Also, it shouldn’t push up against a wall or other gear–you’re your generator well-ventilated on all sides.

Because they don’t emit any exhaust fumes, power stations can be set up wherever you like; however, if you are pairing them with solar panels, you’ll need them to be within cable distance of the panels, and your panels will need to be positioned to capture sunlight.

You can, but you shouldn’t. Electricity and water don’t mix, and running a generator in the rain can have unpredictable results. At best, it may fry the generator or your RV electrical system. At worst, it could cause a fire or electrocute someone.

He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6472. Scientists Reveal How a Mysterious Brain Structure Keeps Memories From Fading

Memories that last only seconds shape everyday thinking, and research in mice is revealing how a small brain structure supports an ability impaired in ADHD and schizophrenia.

To understand a sentence, the brain has to keep earlier words in mind as new ones arrive. Working memory makes that possible, holding information for a few seconds so we can compare it with new information, manipulate it, and use it to guide our behavior.

We rely on it to follow conversations, solve problems, and decide what to do next. Yet sensory information fades within moments once a stimulus ends, leaving the brain with the demanding task of maintaining a usable representation of something that is no longer there.

In mice, researchers at UNIGE have found that this ability relies partly on the claustrum, a thin structure deep within the brain between the insular cortex and the striatum. Their findings appear in Nature Communications.

The scientists tested mice on tasks that required them to remember either a smell or a touch. Each animal received an initial stimulus, waited several seconds, and then received a second stimulus. The mouse had to determine whether the two were identical or different. By the time the second stimulus arrived, the first was gone, so success depended on retaining information about it during the wait.

Temporarily reducing the activity of claustrum neurons cut the mice’s working memory performance in half. To control these neurons at precise moments during the task, the researchers used techniques including optogenetics. This method uses specific proteins to make selected neurons sensitive to light, allowing scientists to alter their activity through an optical fiber. The intervention helped establish that the claustrum contributes to working memory rather than simply becoming active while another brain region does the necessary work.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” says study co-leader Alan Carleton, Full Professor in the Department of Basic Neurosciences at UNIGE’s Faculty of Medicine. “Moreover, disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself.”

Working memory depends on interactions across a broad network that includes the prefrontal cortex, sensory regions, the parietal cortex, the thalamus, and other structures beneath the cortex. These networks must preserve information while allowing the brain to continue perceiving, thinking, and acting, but how they maintain a representation over time remains largely unknown. The claustrum’s anatomy offers a reason to examine its contribution.

“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” explains Carleton.

Recordings from the mice allowed the researchers to examine how information was represented in claustrum activity during the gap between stimuli.

“Our live recordings of claustrum neuron activity showed that a trace of the initial information persisted throughout the entire waiting period,” says fellow study leader Ivan Rodriguez, Full Professor in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE’s Faculty of Science. “Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time. Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”

“Our discovery could help us better understand cognitive disorders in which working memory is impaired, such as schizophrenia or ADHD,” explains Carleton. “Identifying the brain circuits that allow information to be maintained over time is an important step towards understanding how these functions can be disrupted. We now need to determine how the claustrum communicates with cortical networks, and how this interaction preserves the fidelity of the representations held in working memory.”

Reference: “The claustrum contributes to working memory maintenance in mice” by Anindya S. Bhattacharjee, Maxime Juventin, Chieko Huber, Burak Unsal, Jean-Rodolphe Renfer, Ivan Rodriguez and Alan Carleton, 14 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78363-6
