#6428. A 4,000-year-old wall was found hiding underneath a Moroccan ridge that a French archaeologist sketched in the 1930s

Charcoal beneath a wall Armand Ruhlmann recorded in 1936 at Oued Beht, Morocco, dates its first phase to as early as 2010 BC.

In 1936, the French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann published photographs and a sketch of the walls on a ridge at Oued Beht, in Morocco’s Khémisset Province. He took them for a prehistoric enclosure. Under the stones he described, a wall dated about 4,000 years old remained buried.

It turned up in a trench dug by hand across the largest wall during the 2023 field season, which ran from October 30 to November 17. Charcoal from its cobble foundation gave a radiocarbon range of 2010 to 1747 BC.

The trench belongs to the Oued Beht Archaeological Project, with partners in Rabat, Rome and Cambridge. Its results are now out in Libyan Studies.

The paper reports a ditch, an earth bank and a wall from the early to mid-second millennium BC, and it leaves their purpose open.

Four stone alignments run east to west over the southern end of the ridge, above a river that flows all year. The village of Aït Siberne shows to the east in drone photographs taken by Toby Wilkinson of Cambridge.

Ruhlmann tied the biggest alignment, now labeled Wall B1, to a slighter wall on the western scarp and to Wall C further south. He read them as an éperon barré, or barred spur. That is a headland closed off on its open side by a rampart.

Giulio Lucarini of Italy’s National Research Council and Cyprian Broodbank of Cambridge are the corresponding authors of the new paper. They and 19 co-authors call Ruhlmann’s plan a “neat but unproven reconstruction.”

A French and Moroccan project dug into Wall B1 and Wall C between 2013 and 2015. That work is unpublished, and the remnants of its trenches were still open in 2022 and 2023.

Local residents told the team that the upper stonework had been bigger within living memory. The wall had also been turned into a stable for animals.

Trench 3 was laid out as a long slit across Wall B1. Its northern extension, Trench 3.1, was offset to keep clear of an olive tree. Work there stopped at about 4 feet (1.2 meters) for safety.

The visible wall, numbered F.300.2, is about 7.5 feet (2.3 meters) wide at ground level and 4.4 feet (1.35 meters) high. It is built of limestone blocks and cobbles in compacted earth.

Under it lay F.300.1, an older structure of burnt and unburnt daub, a building mud, with ashy lenses full of charcoal. It sat on rounded river or beach cobbles less than 4 inches (10 centimeters) across. All 17 sherds from it were prehistoric.

A second charcoal date, from the burnt material, gave 1896 to 1623 BC. The authors link that layer to the destruction of the first wall.

The team had expected Wall B1 to widen the site’s time range. “This expectation was spectacularly fulfilled,” the authors wrote.

North of the wall, Trench 3.1 ran into a ditch parallel to it. It was about 6 feet (1.84 meters) wide and at least 2 feet (65 centimeters) deep, and its base may not have been reached. One of its fills held a polished stone axe, and all 18 sherds from the ditch were prehistoric.

Bulk soil samples of 10 to 20 liters (about 3 to 5 gallons) went through flotation, which lifts seeds and charcoal off in water. Three charred seeds of domesticated crops from the ditch came back at about 1500 to 1300 BC.

The lowest phase of the earth bank gave 1532 to 1424 BC and 1497 to 1300 BC. A slanted posthole north of the wall, probably for a timber prop, held a legume seed dated to 1502 to 1324 BC.

Altogether the two trenches produced 17 dates, eight on seeds and nine on charcoal. Two charcoal samples with modern results were treated as intrusive and set aside.

The wall line follows the contact between Jurassic dolostone on the south and the Blue Marl Formation on the north. In their conclusions, the authors call the Wall B1 sequence “the earliest such constructions confirmed in the region.” Defense is one reading, but other motives for enclosure “cannot be excluded at this stage,” they wrote.

An earlier paper in Antiquity dated a farming community on the northern ridge to about 3400 to 2900 BC. Its authors called it currently the earliest and largest agricultural complex in Africa beyond the Nile corridor.

After the 2023 survey, that settlement is put at 10 to 11 hectares (25 to 27 acres). It has yielded bell-shaped storage pits, painted pottery and polished stone axes. Plant remains include barley, durum wheat, pea and wild olive.

In the second millennium BC, the activity moved south to the narrow tip. Morocco is better known for far older material, such as shell beads 142,000 to 150,000 years old and hominin jawbones from Casablanca.

The paper sets Oued Beht next to Kach Kouch, a site near the Mediterranean coast. People lived there late in the second millennium BC.

The authors suggest the two may mark a Bronze Age in northwestern Morocco, in step with the Argaric culture, a Bronze Age society in southern Spain. In those centuries, a fire at Cabezo Redondo in Spain preserved a wooden loom.

Medieval builders went back to the same line. Charcoal from the middle phase of the bank gave two dates in the 11th to 12th centuries AD. A stone wall just north of Wall B1 gave the 11th to 13th.

The standing stone wall belongs to that later phase, according to the paper, because the upper layers of the bank probably went up at about the same time. A seed from the fill inside the wall gave 1729 to 1516 BC, which the authors put down to older soil reused as fill.

At the northern edge of the site, local people had reported human remains in 2022, during house building. The team dug three test trenches there. Trench 7 exposed a burial with its skull to the west, and a molar dated it to the 13th century AD.

Across a shallow valley, about 1,640 feet (500 meters) away, survey walkers found a dense spread of 11th to 13th century pottery on a hilltop. One sherd, painted cobalt blue, was likely made in Fez.

Wall C, the southern piece of Ruhlmann’s plan, has no dates. Whether the three walls ever formed one enclosure is still unknown.

A copper-based rod 2.2 inches (5.5 centimeters) long came from the bank south of Wall B1. Its layer has no radiocarbon date, and no Bronze Age metal has been confirmed at Oued Beht so far.

Each radiocarbon date gives the earliest possible age of its layer. Charcoal and seeds can predate the soil that buried them.

Ruhlmann’s 1936 sketch showed Wall B1 as a rampart of unknown age. Its first phase now has two charcoal dates, and the authors have proposed limited work on Wall C.

The project runs under a memorandum of understanding between Morocco’s National Institute of Archaeological Sciences and Heritage, the National Research Council of Italy, ISMEO (the International Association for Mediterranean and Oriental Studies) and Cambridge’s McDonald Institute. The paper thanks the Oukhayi family for letting the team dig on their property.

The full study was published in the journal Libyan Studies.

#6427. Researchers hung baited cameras off a boat and identified 50 different oceanic whitetip sharks using only their fins

Baited cameras off Cat Island, The Bahamas, filmed 50 oceanic whitetip sharks that researchers told apart by dorsal fin markings over two seasons.

In late April 2023, a Florida International University (FIU) crew off Cat Island in The Bahamas started dropping baited GoPro cameras over the side. The goal was to film oceanic whitetip sharks about 43 feet (13 meters) down, with 2 pounds (1 kilogram) of bonito as bait.

They came back in 2024 and did it again. By then the video showed 50 separate whitetips. Each one was picked out by the notches, shape and pigmentation pattern of its first dorsal fin, the tall fin on the back.

Candace Fields, who is Bahamian and got her PhD in marine biology at FIU in 2025, ran the survey. Counting fins sometimes put up to three times as many sharks at a camera as the usual tally. All of it, though, comes from one island and two springs of fieldwork.

According to NOAA Fisheries, oceanic whitetips can reach 11 feet (3.4 meters). They spend most of their time in the top 656 feet (200 meters) of the open ocean.

NOAA puts the drop across the Pacific at about 80 to 95 percent since the mid-1990s. It names bycatch in commercial fisheries and demand for the fins as the main threat, and says some recent recovery is possible in the Pacific.

A Mote Marine Laboratory report found that most species in the shark fin trade are threatened with extinction. The IUCN lists the oceanic whitetip as Critically Endangered, and the U.S. Endangered Species Act lists it as threatened.

Yannis Papastamatiou is an FIU marine biologist at the university’s Institute of Environment and one of Fields’ advisers. “When you’re talking about marine predators in the ocean, that’s very difficult to answer, much harder than with terrestrial predators,” he told FIU News.

“If you want an idea of the abundance of lions, you can do airplane surveys and count them. But in the marine environment, you can’t see things, so that’s very difficult to do.”

FIU researchers had already surveyed another shark species for 10 years at an atoll with baited cameras, FIU News reported. Off Cat Island the water was too deep to anchor cameras to the bottom.

Fields tried two kinds of rig in late April and early May of 2023 and 2024. One was a frame of 3/4-inch galvanized steel pipe holding at least two GoPro Hero9 Black cameras. It drifted on a rope under a float and a flagged marker buoy, with a dive weight underneath.

The other was a wire bait cage with a camera. It hung about 49 feet (15 meters) from a 79-foot (24-meter) Viking sportfishing yacht. In the acknowledgments, the authors thank Captain Scott Genereux for running the Lady G.

The crew put out 99 sets between Columbus Point and Tartar Bank, a shallow seamount west of the island. Of those, 76 hung from the boat and 23 drifted, each at least half a mile (800 meters) from the last. Whitetips came to 51 of them.

Some earlier accounts said whitetips home in on boat engines. In this survey the tethered cage drew no more sharks than the drifting rig. Whether the engine was on or off did not matter either.

More sharks turned up at Columbus Point, a shelf edge where tuna, wahoo and billfish feed in winter and spring. Windy days brought more of them too. The authors think the rigs drifted farther and the scent of bonito spread wider.

Fields told FIU News that reading whitetip fins is similar to reading the spots on a whale shark. In the Western Indian Ocean, photos of those spots helped track individual whale sharks over ten years.

Until now, whitetip photo ID came from divers, who could swim into position for a clean shot. “In a video survey, obviously, you have no means to control how the shark approaches the camera. So, one big question was: is this even viable?” Fields said.

Each time a whitetip came into view, an annotator saved a still of its first dorsal fin. A shark got its own code, such as OWT1, only once both sides of the fin were on camera.

Some sharks circled the rig again and again. Others swam in at angles that hid the markings, and glare and murky water hid more. Still, the team picked out at least one shark by its fin on 41 of the 51 sets with whitetips.

Twenty-five of the 50 sharks got full codes. The other 25 were told apart from the right side of the fin alone.

Twelve sharks were filmed on two or more sets in the same season. Two of them, OWT8 and OWT15, were first filmed in 2023 and came back to the cameras in 2024.

Most camera studies report MaxN, the largest number of one species seen in a single frame. The fin count and MaxN agreed on about 87 percent of sets. Most of those had no whitetip or just one.

With two whitetips on screen at once, the counts matched only 31 percent of the time. With three, it was 28 percent. Papastamatiou said fin IDs let a researcher review the footage and say “actually, that was three different sharks.”

Fields now works at the Cape Eleuthera Institute in Rock Sound, Eleuthera. “I think what FIU did for me was solidify the importance of coming back home to work. The Bahamas is a big hub for shark research, and there are little to no Bahamians involved in that work,” she told FIU News.

Her other adviser, Demian Chapman, now works at Mote Marine Laboratory in Sarasota, Florida. Fields said both men pushed her to stick with it and become a Bahamian shark expert.

The 99 sets are a first count for whitetips in The Bahamas. They say nothing yet about whether the population is rising or falling.

On some sets no fin could be read. In those cases the team used MaxN. On three sets it told sharks apart by sex, a tag or fishing gear hanging from the body. The data are not in a public archive, and the paper says Fields will share them on reasonable request.

The authors also note that The Bahamas is a shark sanctuary but whitetips swim out of it into fished waters. In the Marshall Islands, scientists found that a shark sanctuary offered little protection from illegal fishing.

Next, the team wants cameras at more points along the archipelago, to see whether the sharks stay put or travel between islands. Fields also hopes to add photos from citizen scientists to the fin catalog.

OWT8 and OWT15 first swam up to the bonito off Cat Island in the spring of 2023. A year later both were back.

The full study was published in the journal Marine Biology.

#6425. Foreign visitors to medieval Rome had to change their money, but the Anglo-Saxons kept their coins

Twenty Anglo-Saxon coins dug up beside the Vatican point to a busy English quarter in Rome where English money may have changed hands freely.

An Anglo-Saxon traveler heading for Rome in the ninth century had to think about money before leaving. The city ran on the pope’s coins, and foreign ones were not supposed to be accepted there.

Twenty silver coins from England have now come out of the ground near the Vatican, most of them from rubbish pits. English pilgrims and settlers lost them, one by one, over decades, in the quarter where they lived.

The archaeologists found these Anglo-Saxon coins mixed in with papal and Roman coins, among workshops. The two historians who studied them say the English may have been allowed to spend their own money in Rome.

The finds are also the first physical trace of the English quarter that medieval texts describe.

Rory Naismith studies early medieval England in the Department of Anglo-Saxon, Norse and Celtic at the University of Cambridge. Francesca Tinti is a medieval historian at the University of the Basque Country.

In an interview with Earth.com, Naismith said the two had wondered for years what a dig at one particular church would turn up. Santo Spirito in Sassia sits in the middle of the old English quarter.

“Our hope was that it might produce artifacts and coins from England in the early Middle Ages,” he said.

“The Palazzo della Rovere site is literally across the road from the church, so the surprise (in a way) was that our imagined discoveries turned out to be what was actually found.”

Archaeologists began digging under the walled garden of the Palazzo della Rovere in 2020, while the building was being turned into a hotel. In 2023, the same dig found the remains of the emperor Nero’s theater.

Rome’s state archaeology office, the Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma, directed the excavation, and a team coordinated by Marzia Di Mento did the fieldwork.

Thirty coins came out of the ground, and 23 of them were struck in the tenth century. Twenty were Anglo-Saxon: 19 silver pennies and one halfpenny.

They carry the names of Alfred the Great’s son, Edward the Elder, and his grandsons Æthelstan and Eadred, who ruled between 899 and 955.

Fourteen Anglo-Saxon coins had fused into two lumps of six and eight after a thousand years underground. The pennies Naismith and Tinti could read closely came from East Anglia, Kent, London and the West Midlands.

Alongside them lay a coin probably struck for Pope John X, two from the mint at Pavia in northern Italy, and a handful of Roman bronzes. Around the coins was the debris of leather, bone and metalwork production, spread over at least 32,000 square feet (3,000 square meters).

The coins were not one buried hoard. They lay scattered across five spots, with the two biggest groups in rubbish pits. Each of those groups held Anglo-Saxon, Italian and Roman coins together.

Naismith and Tinti considered whether the silver was being collected to melt down, and found nothing on the site to suggest it. There wasn’t a trace of silver working at all.

The halfpenny pointed the same way, because small change like that turns up rarely in hoards and often where lots of low-value trading went on.

Naismith told Earth.com that each coin was worth tens of modern dollars and was relatively rare in the tenth century.

“People would not have lost them lightly,” he said. “So, to find this many in one place suggests these coins were being used intensively, for lots of transactions. In other words, this was a vibrant area.”

Written records from Rome in this period mention only papal money, and the historians read that as the rule.

Foreign coin was not normally acceptable, and one ninth-century letter mentions a Frankish abbot who worried about changing his currency before a trip to the city.

English silver pennies have turned up in Rome before. One in a hoard from the House of the Vestals in the Forum, and another near the Vatican Radio station.

Until now, though, none had come from the heart of the English quarter itself, the Schola Saxonum, which texts place in this area from the late eighth century.

“The coins aren’t pretty but they have a lot to say,” Naismith said.

“More Anglo-Saxon coins from this period have now been found in Rome than papal coins. This sounds bizarre, but it’s telling us that a very large amount of money was flowing in from England at this time.”

The dates give the historians a clue. The Rome finds cluster between about 900 and 970. That is before the English began the annual payment to the pope known as Peter’s Pence, so the coins are unlikely to be pious offerings.

What was happening instead, Naismith and Tinti suggest, is a deal. Alfred the Great sent alms to Rome in 883 and again in the late 880s.

At Alfred’s request, Pope Marinus I freed the English quarter “from every tribute and toll,” according to Asser, the Welsh scholar who wrote Alfred’s biography in 893.

No surviving source spells out what that privilege covered. The pair propose that the right to spend English money was part of it.

The use of English coin in Rome faded around the 970s, and the historians aren’t sure why.

One possibility they raise is that the popes stopped minting their own coins at about that time. The privilege may have depended on the popes actively running the local money system.

The findings appear as a chapter, written in Italian, in the proceedings of a conference held at Roma Tre University in December 2025. The full catalog of the coins is still to come.

Nobody knows how large the English quarter was, or whether Alfred himself secured the currency arrangement. Asser’s line is the only written hint, and the historians call it a possibility rather than a proof.

Asked by Earth.com what comes next, Naismith said more digging on neighboring sites would be ideal. In a city like Rome, he said, the chance only comes when building or utility work opens the ground, as the hotel project did here.

“The church of S. Spirito in Sassia would be especially interesting to look into further,” he said. Until that ground opens, the coins and craft debris from one garden are the only physical trace of the English quarter anyone has seen.

The full study has not been published in a journal. It appears as a chapter in the book of conference proceedings titled Rome and the Others (300-1000), published by SAP Società Archeologica (ISBN: 9791256820405).

The reentry of NASA's dead Swift space telescope is the end of an era for rapid-response space science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

#6422. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

Sanders: The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. This episode was produced and mixed by Ella Rowen. Our project manager is Ashley Yeager. Nancy Shute is our editor in chief. Our music is by Blue Dot Sessions. The podcast is made possible in part by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund with support from PRX.

#6421. Two decades of tracking data on Manx shearwaters shows the seabirds actually get jet lag just like humans do

GPS tracks of 1,045 Manx shearwaters over 20 years show fast eastward flights leave their body clocks up to an hour behind, bending their sun compass.

Manx shearwaters from Skomer Island, off the Pembrokeshire coast of Wales, sometimes fly about 621 miles (1,000 kilometers) west into the Atlantic to feed. On the flight back east, some go fast enough to get a kind of jet lag.

The sun comes up earlier the farther east a bird is. After a long day flying east, a shearwater’s body clock can run up to an hour behind.

Oxford biologists saw the effect in the birds’ tracks. The steering errors went up to about 15 degrees. The team does not yet know if the lag does the birds any other harm.

Lewin and 23 co-authors published the paper in Science on October 29, 2026. It used 20 years of GPS data from 1,045 Manx shearwaters on 3,688 foraging trips.

Professor Tim Guilford, a co-author, belongs to the Oxford Navigation Group, which works mostly on Skomer and on Lighthouse Island in County Down.

The group’s GPS loggers were first designed for geotagging photos on backpacking trips, its project page says. Team members take them apart and wrap them in heat-shrink plastic.

The birds came from seven colonies. The R code the team put on Zenodo lists Skomer, Skokholm, Ramsey, Lundy, Copeland, Rum and St Kilda. Skomer has nearly 350,000 breeding pairs, the Wildlife Trust of South and West Wales says.

In the code, every track was cut down to one GPS fix every five minutes. A trip home only counted if it started at least 31 miles (50 kilometers) out. It also had to end at least 25 percent closer.

Birds that use the sun as a compass also need to know the time. The sun moves across the sky all day. Normally they set their body clock at sunrise, the University of Oxford said.

A drawing released with the paper shows how this goes wrong. In it, a shearwater starts for home at 30 degrees west. Its clock matches local time there.

Six hours later the bird is at 15 degrees west, where the sun came up an hour sooner. The sun now sits about 20 degrees clockwise of where the bird expects it. So the bird turns about 20 degrees clockwise of its proper heading.

Birds in the GPS records drifted clockwise as they flew east. Dr. Patrick Lewin of Oxford’s Department of Biology, who led the work, said that is the pattern a clock running late would produce.

For each fix, the code works out where the sun would be from the spot where the bird saw sunrise that day. Crosswind and distance from the colony go into the models as well.

Magnetic values for every fix came from the International Geomagnetic Reference Field, via a program called geomag70. The sun model beat the magnetic one.

In Japan, streaked shearwaters were used to study how birds rely on an inner compass tied to magnetic sensing.

Lewin said it is “amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction.”

The code also checks whether a straight line from each fix to the colony crosses land.

A comment in the code says the team had to leave out points around St. David’s Head for Skomer and Skokholm. Without that step, every point to the north would count as having no clear line home because of a small stretch of land.

Along coasts the birds kept making the same errors, flying nearer the shore when the predicted error pointed toward land and farther out when it pointed out to sea.

Guilford, a co-author, said the thinking of wild animals is hard to study. Measuring their natural movements carefully, he said, “can reveal the underlying behavioral mechanisms.”

The team worked out one case for an adult bird. It started 621 miles (1,000 kilometers) out with an average error of 7 degrees. It corrected its course all the way.

That bird would fly only about 3.1 miles (5 kilometers) extra before getting within 3.1 miles of its colony.

A young bird on its first migration may not correct like that, Lewin’s group said. Its errors could add up to hundreds of kilometers. Caspian terns do not fly that first trip alone, because fathers lead young birds on their first migration.

Manx shearwaters spend the northern winter off Argentina, according to the Oxford group. Another Oxford-led study reported that the endangered Balearic shearwater changed its migration range mostly through individual flexibility.

People who fly fast across time zones get disturbed sleep and fatigue, according to the Oxford statement, and jet lag can also unsettle the gut and other organs.

The statement says more research is needed on whether wild birds suffer any effects on health, behavior or survival. The hundreds of kilometers for young birds came from a calculation.

Lewin wants to find out what the lag does to them. “Do they mistime critical behaviors? Do they experience physiological side effects like we do?” he said in the University of Oxford statement.

Lewin also said the shearwaters, which make long flights all the time, might one day help people deal with jet lag. For now, they keep racing an earlier sunrise back to Skomer.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6420. The Sky This Week from November 6 to 13: Venus in the spotlight

Friday, November 6The waning Moon leaves us with perfect skies for deep-sky observing. Let’s kick off the week with a bright planetary nebula in Aquarius: NGC 7293, commonly known as the Helix Nebula.

Despite its impressive magnitude of 7.3, the Helix presents a challenge: It is a broad 13’ across, which spreads its light over a relatively large part of sky, lowering its overall surface brightness. That said, you can still find the Helix in large binoculars or any small scope, tucked into southeastern Aquarius, roughly 7.7° southwest of magnitude 3.3 Skat (Delta [δ] Aquarii). If you turn south around 7 P.M. local time, find Skat to the upper right of bright Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus, then scan to its lower right, toward 5th-magnitude 66 Aqr. That star lies about halfway between Skat and the Helix Nebula.

Once you’ve located the Helix, the more magnification you can turn on it, the better. Larger amateur scopes will start to show structure in the ring of glowing gas surrounding the central white dwarf, with the northern and southern edges glowing brighter than the eastern and western sides. That gas was once part of the central star, which puffed up and blew away its outer layers as it aged. Sunrise: 6:35 A.M. Sunset: 4:52 P.M. Moonrise: 3:56 A.M. Moonset: 3:16 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)

Saturday, November 7Venus is our (morning) star of the week, capturing attention above the eastern horizon before sunrise. This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Earth’s sister planet at 7 A.M. EST.

You can easily catch the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up.

Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight. This morning it lies 1.3° northeast of Venus, with the planet and star roughly side by side above the horizon. Use this view as an anchor point: By the 10th, Venus will have moved to stand due west of this star and will be located to its upper right.

Sunrise: 6:36 A.M. Sunset: 4:51 P.M. Moonrise: 5:01 A.M. Moonset: 3:40 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (1%)

Sunday, November 8Rising with the stars of western Leo shortly before midnight, bright Jupiter and its Galilean moons put on a show early this morning, better visible the farther east you’re located.

Jupiter is just under 5° northwest (to the upper right) of Regulus as they rise in the east. Fainter Mars stands roughly 3° above Jupiter. You’ll want your telescope trained on the gas giant soon after rising to catch the show, which begins at 1:29 A.M. EST as a shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb. This is Io’s shadow — but don’t be fooled by the positions of the moons you see in your scope. The moon closest to Jupiter on the east is Callisto, while the moon just east of that is Io, whose shadow we see. Ganymede lies farthest east, while Europa is currently hidden behind the planet in an occultation. The latter appears from behind the eastern limb about 1:54 A.M. EST, not long before Callisto reaches the planet and begins a transit at 2:07 A.M. EST.

Keep an eye on Io and Europa: Io passes north of Europa at 2:23 A.M. EST, then heads into its own transit about 2:42 A.M. EST. Now the race is on, as Io approaches and then catches up with Callisto as the two moons transit, passing Callisto and moving west of it within half an hour. The two moons and Io’s shadow continue to transit until 3:45 A.M. EST, when Io’s shadow leaves the western limb, and Io takes about an hour and a quarter longer before egress. Callisto continues trundling along, finally finishing its transit about 5:51 A.M. CST, with the sky now starting to brighten with twilight in the Midwest.

Sunrise: 6:37 A.M. Sunset: 4:50 P.M. Moonrise: 6:07 A.M. Moonset: 4:08 P.M. Moon Phase: New

Monday, November 9New Moon occurs at 2:02 A.M. EST. Dark skies make tonight the perfect opportunity to try spotting Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS, still nearly 50° above the western horizon two hours after sunset.

Glowing around 10th magnitude, the comet is currently located in far northern Aquila, near the Eagle’s border with Sagitta the Arrow. You can use Aquila’s bright luminary, Altair, to guide your way — the comet floats 7.7° north-northeast of this star. A closer but fainter guide is 4th-magnitude Alpha (α) Sagittae, just 2.3° north of the comet’s position tonight. Even a small scope will nab you the comet, but larger apertures will yield better views. Under high magnification, look at the comet’s southern side, which should be sharper as it plows into the solar wind.

Not far from Hartley-IRAS’ position is the famous Coathanger asterism, located in Vulpecula the Fox. Cataloged as Collinder 399, you’ll find it roughly 5° northwest of the comet’s position, or about 4° northwest of Alpha Sge. Visible in binoculars or any telescope (in this case, lower magnification is better), you’ll immediately see why this star pattern bears its name. It looks exactly like its namesake, with a line of stars bisected by a small curve extending to the south. At the Coathanger’s eastern edge lies the open cluster NGC 6802.

Sunrise: 6:38 A.M. Sunset: 4:49 P.M. Moonrise: 7:12 A.M. Moonset: 4:40 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (1%)

Tuesday, November 10The waxing crescent Moon passes 0.3° south of Antares at midnight EST, although the pair is not visible at that time. You can catch our satellite setting in the west around sunset, although it will likely disappear before Antares pops out of the twilight — that will likely happen only shortly before the star itself sets as well.

Instead, challenge yourself with a different type of observation: picking up Saturn’s moon Iapetus, which tonight reaches greatest eastern elongation 9.4’ east of the ringed planet. The two-toned moon is tidally locked to its parent world, which means it rotates in time with its orbit. At eastern elongation, Iapetus’ darker hemisphere faces earthward, reducing the moon’s magnitude to nearly 12. This, combined with its distance from Saturn, makes it more of a challenge to find, but you can give it a try if you’ve got a larger scope.

Try around 9 P.M. local time when Saturn is highest, some 50° above the southern horizon. It’s the brightest point of light in this region of the sky, hanging just below Pisces and to the far upper left of Fomalhaut, the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus (much closer to the horizon). Even if you can’t locate Iapetus or don’t have a large scope, Saturn is magnificent through a telescope. Its disk spans 19” and its rings are roughly 43” across, showing off their southern side. You should definitely spot its largest and brightest moon, mid-8th-magnitude Titan, just over 2’ west of the planet. Depending on your scope and when you look, you may also spot at least three other moons: 10th-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea, closer to the planet. Tethys lies to Saturn’s west, while Rhea and Dione are to the east.

Sunrise: 6:39 A.M. Sunset: 4:48 P.M. Moonrise: 8:15 A.M. Moonset: 5:19 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (4%)

Wednesday, November 11Venus reaches a stationary point among the stars of Virgo at 10 A.M. EST. This brings its retrograde (westward) motion to an end; after today, Venus will begin moving eastward or prograde through the sky, swinging north of Spica.

You can easily catch the bright planet in the eastern sky before dawn. Venus’ brightness has increased over just the past few days, and it now blazes at magnitude –4.7. An hour before sunrise, you’ll easily spot it alongside Spica, standing just to the star’s upper right. Both are 10° high and rising as dawn approaches. Check out Venus through a telescope: its disk shows off a crescent phase just 10% lit, but stretches an impressive 53” in the sky.

Also just becoming visible at this time is Mercury, barely 1.5° above the horizon and glowing at magnitude 1.2. See if you can locate it about 13° east (to the lower left) of Venus, although you’ll need a particularly flat horizon free of trees, buildings, and lights. Mercury, too, rises as twilight brightens, which may make the planet harder to see in the growing light. Try scanning for it with binoculars, although make sure to put them away well before sunrise from your location, which may differ from the time given below.

Sunrise: 6:41 A.M. Sunset: 4:47 P.M. Moonrise: 9:15 A.M. Moonset: 6:05 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (8%)

Thursday, November 12The constellation Perseus is famous for its bright Double Cluster, but these two open clusters aren’t the only groups of young stars in the Hero worth viewing. Today, let’s shift our gaze to the western portion of this constellation, near its border with Andromeda, to check out M34, a mid-5th-magnitude open cluster containing about 100 stars.

Sitting 5.2° west-northwest of 2nd-magnitude Algol (Beta [β] Persei), M34 spans about half a degree, roughly the size of the Full Moon. In physical space, astronomers believe the group spans about 14 light-years and sits 1,400 light-years away. It’s best seen under lower magnifications, such as in binoculars or small amateur scopes (4 inches or so). You’ll spot several dozen stars brighter than 12th magnitude, with its brightest suns spread throughout the cluster.

Sunrise: 6:42 A.M. Sunset: 4:46 P.M. Moonrise: 10:08 A.M. Moonset: 6:57 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (14%)

Friday, November 13The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

Celebrate Friday the 13th with something spooky: a ghost in the constellation Andromeda. This evening, point your telescope toward 2nd-magnitude Mirach (Beta [β] Andromedae), already nearly 60° high in the east by 7 P.M. local time. One of the Princess’ brightest stars, Mirach is a cool, reddish M-type giant. It lies some 200 light-years away and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly as our Sun.

But Mirach is not quite our target — we’re looking for its so-called ghost, just 6.8’ northwest of the star. You’ll need a big scope to see it, but look carefully: Can you spot a faint smudge of light, about 4’ across, close to the star? This is the Ghost of Mirach, a far more distant elliptical galaxy glowing at 10th magnitude and cataloged as NGC 404. It lies some 8 million to 10 million light-years away, just beyond the gravitational bounds of our Local Group of galaxies. It’s called a ghost because it appears almost like a ghostly image of the bright star Mirach, which dominates the view.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M. Sunset: 4:45 P.M. Moonrise: 10:54 A.M. Moonset: 7:55 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%)

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.
